Disavow

/dis-uh-VOW/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Disavow means to deny knowledge of, responsibility for, or association with something.

Disavow means to deny knowledge of, responsibility for, or association with something. The candidate moved quickly to disavow the insulting flyer, insisting that no one on her staff had approved it.

Worked Example

When a wellness blog claimed his sleep study proved that naps cure illness, Dr. Ferro published a letter to disavow the claim. He explained that his research had never tested anything of the kind, and he wanted no association with the exaggeration.

Dr. Ferro publicly denies any connection between himself and the blog's claim, which is exactly what it means to disavow something.

How Disavow Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

Antonyms

acknowledge

endorse

endorse: to publicly support or approve

How Strong Is It? — deny → disavow → repudiate

deny vs. disavow

deny vs. disavow: To deny is the everyday act of saying something is not true, while to disavow is a more formal, public refusal to be connected with it.

repudiate vs. disavow

repudiate vs. disavow: To disavow is to deny any association, but to repudiate is even stronger, a complete and often dramatic rejection of the thing itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: not, opposite of

Root — avow

Root — avow: to declare or affirm openly

Put it together

Put it together: Disavow pairs dis-, meaning not or opposite of, with avow, to declare or affirm openly, which traces back to the Latin votum, a vow. To disavow is literally to un-declare something, taking back any claim of connection.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / public statements

Disavow almost always describes a public, on-the-record denial, often by an official, an organization, or a public figure. If you privately doubt something, you are merely skeptical; when you formally announce you have no part in it, you disavow it.
